questions.title: Give Jane read access to Pods
questions.scenario: In namespace 'dev', user 'jane' must be able to get and list Pods - nothing more, and only in that namespace.
questions.tip: Role/RoleBinding are namespaced; ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding are cluster-wide. Always finish with 'kubectl auth can-i'.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Create the namespaced permission set (a Role) named 'pod-reader'. Type the correct command in full.

options.why: A ClusterRole is cluster-scoped: '-n' is ignored and the object is not limited to 'dev'.
No '-n dev': the Role lands in the current namespace (usually 'default').
The flags are singular: --verb and --resource.

s1.explain: 'kubectl create role NAME --verb=... --resource=... -n NS' generates the rule imperatively - far faster than writing YAML.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Bind that Role to user 'jane' (binding name: read-pods).

options.why: It references a ClusterRole, but 'pod-reader' is a Role: the binding would grant nothing.
A ClusterRoleBinding has no --role flag; it can only bind ClusterRoles.
--serviceaccount expects 'namespace:name' and targets ServiceAccounts, not users.

s2.explain: A RoleBinding grants a Role (or ClusterRole) inside ONE namespace to users, groups or ServiceAccounts.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Verify that jane can list Pods in 'dev'.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=jane -n dev
kubectl auth can-i list pods --user=jane -n dev
options.why: --user picks a credential entry in your kubeconfig; impersonation is done with --as.
'can-i' is a sub-command of 'auth'.

options.cmd: kubectl auth can-i pods list --as=jane -n dev
options.why: Order matters: verb first, then resource.

s3.explain: '--as' impersonates a user. The answer is simply 'yes' or 'no'.

questions.title: Upgrade a worker node
questions.scenario: The control plane already runs v1.37.1. Upgrade worker 'node01' to v1.37.1 (Pods are running on it). The kubeadm package on node01 is already upgraded.
questions.tip: Worker upgrade order: drain -> kubeadm upgrade node -> upgrade kubelet/kubectl packages + restart kubelet -> uncordon.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - From the control plane: safely evict the workloads from node01 and make it unschedulable.

options.why: Cordon only marks the node unschedulable; running Pods are NOT evicted.
Refuses to proceed when DaemonSet Pods (CNI, kube-proxy) or emptyDir volumes exist: it needs the two extra flags.
Removes the Node object entirely; the node would have to re-join the cluster.

s1.explain: drain = cordon + evict. DaemonSet Pods cannot be evicted (--ignore-daemonsets) and emptyDir data is lost (--delete-emptydir-data).

s2.prompt: Step 2 - On node01 (after ssh): upgrade its local kubelet configuration.

options.why: 'apply' is only for the FIRST control-plane node.
'plan' only reports the available versions; it changes nothing.

s2.explain: On workers (and additional control-plane nodes) it is 'kubeadm upgrade node'. Afterwards you upgrade the kubelet package and run 'systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet'.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The kubelet is upgraded and restarted. From the control plane, let node01 receive Pods again.

options.why: That is the opposite: it makes the node unschedulable.
There is no such command.

s3.explain: A drained node stays SchedulingDisabled until you uncordon it - the classic forgotten last step.

questions.title: Deployment with resource limits
questions.scenario: Create a Deployment 'web' (image nginx:1.26, 3 replicas) whose container is limited to cpu 500m and memory 128Mi.
questions.tip: For anything the imperative command cannot express: generate with '--dry-run=client -o yaml', edit, then apply.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Generate the manifest into deploy.yaml WITHOUT creating anything in the cluster.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26 --replicas=3 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

options.why: 'kubectl run' creates a Pod, not a Deployment.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26 --replicas=3 -o yaml > deploy.yaml
options.why: Without --dry-run=client the Deployment is created immediately in the cluster.

options.cmd: kubectl create deployment web --image nginx:1.26 --replicas 3 --dry-run -o yaml > deploy.yaml
options.why: A bare --dry-run is not valid any more: it needs a value (client, server or none).

s1.explain: Tip: 'export do="--dry-run=client -o yaml"' saves a lot of typing during the exam.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Limit the container to cpu 500m and memory 128Mi: type the right snippet in place of 'resources: {}'. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: 'limits:' must be a child of 'resources:' (indented 2 more spaces).
'cpu: 500m' must be under limits (2 more spaces).
'memory: 128Mi' must be under limits (2 more spaces).

options.why: 'limits' is at the same level as 'resources': it becomes an unknown container field and nothing is limited.
requests = what the scheduler reserves. The task asks for limits = the maximum the container may use.
128M is SI (128,000,000 bytes); the task says 128Mi (134,217,728 bytes). Watch the suffix.

s2.recap: Replace 'resources: {}' with a resources/limits block (cpu 500m, memory 128Mi).
s2.explain: Limits live under spec.template.spec.containers[].resources. Indentation is everything in YAML: 2 spaces, never tabs.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Create the Deployment from the file.

options.why: -k expects a directory containing a kustomization.yaml, not a manifest file.
The file must be passed with -f.
'replace' fails when the object does not exist yet.

s3.explain: 'apply -f' works both for creation and updates.

questions.title: Reserve a node for GPU workloads
questions.scenario: Node 'node01' is reserved for GPU workloads. Only Pods that tolerate dedicated=gpu may be scheduled there.
questions.tip: Taint = repel. Toleration = permission to ignore a taint (it does NOT attract the Pod; use nodeSelector/affinity for that).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Taint node01 with key 'dedicated', value 'gpu' and effect NoSchedule.

options.why: The format is key=value:effect - the effect follows a colon.
Labels attract (via selectors/affinity), they never repel. 'gpu:NoSchedule' is not even a valid label value.
The resource type 'nodes' is missing before the node name.

s1.explain: Taint format: key=value:effect. Effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute (also evicts running Pods).

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Make this Pod tolerate dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.
prefill: # TODO: let this Pod run on the tainted node

checks.msg: Add 'tolerations:' directly under 'spec:' (2 spaces of indentation).
tolerations is a LIST: each toleration starts with '- '.

forbid.msg: 'Exists' must not have a value; with 'value: gpu' you need operator Equal (or omit the operator).
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

target: # TODO: let this Pod run on the tainted node

options.why: operator Exists must NOT have a value (the API rejects it). Use Equal + value, or Exists without value.
nodeSelector ATTRACTS the Pod to nodes labelled dedicated=gpu; it does not tolerate the taint: the Pod stays Pending.
tolerations is a list: without '- ' this is a map and the API rejects the Pod.

s2.recap: Add a 'tolerations' list under spec with key/operator/value/effect.
s2.explain: tolerations is a sibling of 'containers' under the Pod spec. Remember: it allows scheduling on the node, it does not force it.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - The reservation is over. Remove the taint from node01.

options.why: There is no --remove flag: a trailing '-' removes a taint.
There is no 'untaint' command.
That removes a LABEL called 'dedicated', not a taint.

s3.explain: Trailing dash = remove, for taints and labels alike.

questions.title: A PVC stuck in Pending
questions.scenario: PVC 'data-pvc' is Pending. PV 'data-pv' exists: capacity 10Gi, accessModes ReadWriteOnce, storageClassName 'manual'. The PVC manifest is pvc.yaml.
questions.tip: To bind, a PV must match the PVC's storageClassName, offer at least the requested size and include the requested access mode.

context: NAME       STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   AGE
s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show why the claim is not binding (conditions and events).

options.why: A PVC is not a workload: it has no logs.
It only repeats the table columns - no events, no reasons.
The volume is fine; the explanation (events) is on the unbound claim.

s1.explain: 'describe' = the Events section is where the scheduler/provisioner tells you what is wrong. First reflex for any Pending object.

context: no persistent volumes available for this claim and no storage class is set
s2.prompt: Step 2 - The claim asks for more than the PV offers (size AND access mode). Type the right snippet over the wrong lines of pvc.yaml.

checks.msg: The PV only offers ReadWriteOnce: the claim must request exactly that.
The PV has 10Gi: request 10Gi or less.

forbid.msg: ReadWriteMany is not offered by the PV.

options.why: The size fits now, but the PV does not offer ReadWriteMany: still no match.
A PVC must state its size in resources.requests.storage; 'limits' alone is rejected.

s2.recap: Set accessModes to ReadWriteOnce and the request to at most 10Gi.
s2.explain: Binding rules: same storageClassName, PV capacity >= request, PV accessModes must include the requested ones.

s3.prompt: Step 3 - Apply the fix. (A PVC's spec cannot be changed in place for these fields.)

options.cmd: kubectl delete pvc data-pvc && kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml

options.why: The API rejects changes to accessModes/size of an existing claim in this state: delete and recreate.
Same immutability problem as apply.

options.cmd: kubectl delete pv data-pv && kubectl apply -f pvc.yaml
options.why: You would delete the volume instead of fixing the claim.

s3.explain: Pending claims have nothing to lose: delete and recreate.

questions.title: Allow API -> DB on port 5432
questions.scenario: Namespace 'prod' has a default-deny ingress policy. Pods labelled app=db must accept TCP 5432 only from Pods labelled app=api (same namespace).
questions.tip: Within one 'from' list, separate items are OR-ed; selectors inside ONE item are AND-ed. An empty rule '- {}' allows everything!

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Add the ingress rule: type the right snippet in place of the TODO comment. Ctrl+D to submit.

checks.msg: Allow traffic 'from' a podSelector with matchLabels app: api.

forbid.msg: An empty ingress rule allows (or denies) the wrong traffic - it must name the source and the port.
'- ports:' starts a SECOND rule: 'ports' must belong to the same rule as 'from' (no dash).
The TODO comment is still there - type the snippet in its place.

options.why: '- ports' starts a second rule. Rules are OR-ed: api may reach ANY port, and EVERYONE may reach 5432.
namespaceSelector selects NAMESPACES labelled app=api, not the api Pods.

s1.recap: Add ingress: from podSelector app=api + ports TCP 5432.
s1.explain: Two selectors: spec.podSelector = who is PROTECTED (db); from.podSelector = who is ALLOWED (api).

s2.prompt: Step 2 - The policy is applied. Show the rules it enforces.

options.cmd: kubectl get netpol allow-api-to-db -n prod -o wide
options.why: 'wide' only shows name, pod-selector and age - not the rules.
A NetworkPolicy has no logs.
'explain' documents the API schema; it does not read live objects.

s2.explain: 'netpol' is the short name for networkpolicies. describe prints the allowed sources and ports in plain language.

questions.title: Expose a Deployment outside the cluster
questions.scenario: Deployment 'web' (label app=web) listens on container port 8080. Expose it as Service 'web-svc' on port 80, reachable from outside through every node.
questions.tip: port = Service port, targetPort = container port. A Service without endpoints means the selector matches no Ready Pod.

options.why: port and target-port are swapped: the container listens on 8080.
The default type is ClusterIP: internal only.
Needs a cloud load balancer (stays <pending> on kubeadm clusters). The task asks for NodePort.

s1.explain: expose copies the selector of the Deployment, so you never write it by hand.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Check that the Service actually targets Ready Pods (list its endpoints).

options.why: That flag does not exist.
'web-svc' is a Service, not a Pod.
EndpointSlices have a random suffix (web-svc-xxxxx), so the exact name is not found; use -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-svc.

s2.explain: An empty ENDPOINTS column (<none>) = wrong selector, wrong namespace or Pods not Ready.

questions.title: A Pod in CrashLoopBackOff
questions.tip: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, not a cause: 'describe' for the reason/exit code, 'logs --previous' for the app's last words.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show the container's last termination reason and exit code.

options.why: Prints application output, not the termination reason or exit code.
Only adds the node and IP columns.
Shows live usage; a crash-looping Pod usually has no metrics.

s1.explain: Look at 'Last State: Terminated' (Reason, Exit Code) and at the Events at the bottom.

s2.prompt: Step 2 - Exit code 137 + OOMKilled = memory limit too low (needs >= 256Mi). Type the right snippet over the resources block.

options.why: The OOM killer enforces the LIMIT, not the request. And request > limit is rejected by the API.
256M is SI (256,000,000 bytes, about 244Mi): below the required 256Mi. Use the binary suffix Mi.
Removing the limit hides the problem: the task asks for a limit of at least 256Mi, and unlimited Pods can starve the node.

s2.recap: Raise resources.limits.memory to >= 256Mi, then recreate the Pod.
s2.explain: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). The kernel killed the process because it exceeded its cgroup memory limit. Keep requests <= limits.

questions.title: A NotReady worker node
questions.scenario: Node 'node01' is NotReady. Walk from the cluster view down to the root cause on the node, then fix it.
questions.tip: The kubelet is NOT a Pod: it is a systemd service on the node. NotReady almost always means 'kubelet stopped talking to the API server'.

s1.prompt: Step 1 - Show node01's Conditions and recent Events.

options.why: kubectl logs only works on Pods (and workload resources).
Needs metrics-server and a working kubelet - a NotReady node reports nothing.
Same table plus IPs and versions: no conditions, no events.

s1.explain: Look for 'Ready False ... Kubelet stopped posting node status' in Conditions.

context: Ready   Unknown   NodeStatusUnknown   Kubelet stopped posting node status.
s2.prompt: Step 2 - ssh to node01: check whether the kubelet service is running.

options.why: The unit is called 'kubelet'.
The kubelet is a systemd service on the node, not a Pod.
kubectl is a client CLI, not a service.

s2.explain: Control-plane components run as static Pods, but the kubelet (and the container runtime) run as systemd services.

context: ● kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent
s3.prompt: Step 3 - Read the last 50 kubelet log lines (no pager).

options.why: There is no kubelet Pod to read logs from.
A unit is selected with -u.
On systemd hosts (kubeadm installs) the kubelet logs to journald.

s3.explain: journalctl -u <unit> is the tool for every systemd component: kubelet, containerd, ...

context: Stopped kubelet.service - kubelet: The Kubernetes Node Agent.
s4.prompt: Step 4 - The service was stopped and disabled. Start it now AND make it survive a reboot.

options.why: Starts it now, but it stays disabled: after a reboot the node is NotReady again.
Survives a reboot, but is not started right now.
Destroys the node's cluster state: a very drastic, unneeded step.

s4.explain: enable --now = enable + start in one command. Then confirm with 'kubectl get nodes' from the control plane.

questions.title: Pods cannot resolve Service names
questions.scenario: Pods report 'bad address' when resolving Service names. Test DNS, inspect CoreDNS, then fix its configuration.
questions.tip: CoreDNS Pods carry the label k8s-app=kube-dns and live in kube-system. Their config is the 'coredns' ConfigMap (the Corefile).

s1.prompt: Step 1 - From a throw-away busybox:1.36 Pod named 'dnstest', resolve kubernetes.default. The Pod must vanish afterwards and its output must be shown.

options.why: Without -it --rm you see no output and the Pod stays behind (Completed).
Assumes a Pod 'dnstest' already exists.
ping tests ICMP, and Service IPs are virtual and do not answer it. nslookup/dig test DNS itself.

s1.explain: --rm -it --restart=Never is the standard throw-away debug Pod pattern.

context: ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
s2.prompt: Step 2 - Read the logs of the CoreDNS Pods.

options.why: No Pod is named exactly 'coredns' (names carry a random suffix); select by label instead.
Missing '-n kube-system': it would search the current namespace.
kubeadm labels CoreDNS Pods k8s-app=kube-dns, even though they are named coredns.

s2.explain: Selecting by label (-l) avoids having to look up the Pod names.

context: [ERROR] plugin/errors: 2 HINFO: read udp 10.244.0.5:40841->10.255.255.1:53: i/o timeout
s3.prompt: Step 3 - 'kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system': upstream queries go to a dead IP. Type the right line in place of the broken 'forward' line.

checks.msg: Do not remove the 'kubernetes' plugin: it serves the cluster domain.

forbid.msg: The dead upstream 10.255.255.1 is still configured.

options.why: Works only with Internet access and bypasses the node's DNS settings (internal domains break). The task asks for the node's resolver file.
Missing the zone: the syntax is 'forward FROM TO...', and FROM '.' means every name.
The 'proxy' plugin was removed from CoreDNS long ago; 'forward' replaced it.

s3.explain: 'kubernetes' answers *.cluster.local; everything else goes through 'forward'. The 'reload' plugin picks up ConfigMap changes within ~2 minutes (or: kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system).
